title: Binary & Bits
tagline: How two symbols — 0 and 1 — encode every number, image, and program you have ever used.

sections.content:
Open any photo on your phone and underneath the pixels is a river of 0s and 1s. Play a song — same river. Run a Python script — the interpreter is itself compiled down to those same two symbols. **Every bit of information a computer touches is ultimately represented in binary.** It is the single most foundational idea in computing, and once you genuinely understand it, a dozen other concepts — from memory addressing to cryptography to floating-point bugs — suddenly make sense.

A **bit** (binary digit) is the smallest unit of information: one symbol that is either 0 or 1. That might sound embarrassingly simple, but the beauty is that two states are all you need. Given enough bits and clever arrangements, you can encode any number, any character, any colour, any instruction.

Binary is not magic — it is just the **base-2 number system**, the same positional place-value idea you learned for decimal, only the base is 2 instead of 10. This chapter will build from first principles: why two states, how place value works, how to convert between bases, what bytes and nibbles are, and why programmers reach for hexadecimal. By the end you will be able to decode a raw byte by eye.

A quick orientation before we dive in: we will cover (1) why two states, (2) place value in base 2, (3) counting in binary, (4) converting between decimal and binary, (5) hexadecimal as shorthand, (6) bytes, kilobytes, and the modern memory units that affect every program you write, and (7) a handful of practical programming patterns that directly follow from this understanding.

sections.caption: The hierarchy of data units — everything starts at the transistor, the physical two-state switch.

sections.title: The Odometer in a Different Base
sections.content:
Imagine a mechanical car odometer. Each wheel can show 10 symbols (0–9). When a wheel rolls past 9 it flips back to 0 and nudges the wheel to its left — a carry. That is base-10 positional counting.

Now build the same machine but give each wheel only **two** symbols: 0 and 1. The wheels fill up much faster: the rightmost wheel starts at 0, flips to 1, and immediately carries into the next wheel on the very next tick. You get the sequence 0, 1, 10, 11, 100, 101, 110, 111, 1000 — which is 0 through 8 in decimal.

The mechanism is identical to decimal counting. Only the number of symbols per wheel changes. Two-symbol wheels are cheap to build from electronics because a switch is either open or closed — nature gives us that duality for free.

sections.title: Why Two States? The Physics of Transistors
sections.content:
The choice of binary is not arbitrary — it falls directly out of how transistors work. A transistor is a semiconductor device that acts as a voltage-controlled switch. When the control voltage is above a threshold, current flows freely (ON); below it, current is blocked (OFF). Two unambiguous states.

Engineers could try to build **multi-valued logic** — distinguish five voltage levels and encode base-5 arithmetic. Some experimental ternary computers have been built (the Soviet Setun in 1958 used balanced ternary). But in practice, noise on electrical lines — from thermal vibration, interference, manufacturing variation — blurs voltage levels together. Distinguishing only two states (high vs. low) gives enormous noise margins. You can tolerate a lot of variation and still be certain which state you are in.

Modern CPUs pack **billions of transistors** onto a chip the size of a fingernail. At that density, simplicity and noise-tolerance are not merely nice-to-have — they are existential engineering requirements. Binary wins because it is robustly physical.

And because each transistor encodes exactly one bit, the entire edifice of computing — registers, RAM, disks, networks — is built from two-state switches in vast combinations.

sections.title: Place Value: How Binary Numbers Actually Work
sections.content:
Positional notation is the key insight. In decimal, the number **305** does not mean 3, 0, and 5 sitting next to each other — it means:

3 × 10² + 0 × 10¹ + 5 × 10⁰ = 300 + 0 + 5 = 305

Each digit is multiplied by a **power of the base** (10) determined by its position. Position 0 is the rightmost, 1 is the next, and so on.

Binary is the same idea with base **2**. The powers of 2 are: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512, 1024 … Every binary digit is multiplied by the corresponding power of 2:

**1011₂** = 1×2³ + 0×2² + 1×2¹ + 1×2⁰ = 8 + 0 + 2 + 1 = **11₁₀**

Notice the subscripts — we use ₂ to mean base 2 and ₁₀ to mean base 10. In code you will often see `0b1011` (Python/JS prefix for binary literals).

A key observation: each position to the left is worth **twice** the previous. Start at 1 (2⁰) and keep doubling: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128. Memorise these eight values and you can convert any byte mentally.

sections.caption: One byte: 8 bit positions, each worth exactly double the one to its right. All eight bits set = 128+64+32+16+8+4+2+1 = 255.

sections.title: Counting in Binary: The Full Pattern
sections.content:
Let us count from 0 to 15 in binary to build intuition:

| Decimal | Binary | Hex |
|---------|--------|-----|
| 0  | 0000 | 0 |
| 1  | 0001 | 1 |
| 2  | 0010 | 2 |
| 3  | 0011 | 3 |
| 4  | 0100 | 4 |
| 5  | 0101 | 5 |
| 6  | 0110 | 6 |
| 7  | 0111 | 7 |
| 8  | 1000 | 8 |
| 9  | 1001 | 9 |
| 10 | 1010 | A |
| 11 | 1011 | B |
| 12 | 1100 | C |
| 13 | 1101 | D |
| 14 | 1110 | E |
| 15 | 1111 | F |

Notice the **patterns**: the rightmost bit alternates every 1 step. The second bit alternates every 2 steps. The third every 4. The fourth every 8. Each bit's period is a power of two — a direct consequence of the doubling place values.

Also notice: with **n bits** you can represent 2ⁿ distinct values, from 0 to 2ⁿ − 1. Four bits → 2⁴ = 16 values (0–15). Eight bits → 2⁸ = 256 values (0–255). This relationship is fundamental and will reappear whenever you think about data sizes, address spaces, and type limits.

sections.title: Converting Decimal to Binary: Two Methods
sections.content:
**Method 1: Repeated subtraction (greedy from the top)**

Find the largest power of 2 that fits into your number. Subtract it and mark a 1 in that position. Repeat with the remainder. Mark 0 for any power that does not fit.

Example — convert **42**:
- 2⁶=64 > 42, skip → 0
- 2⁵=32 ≤ 42, use it, remainder = 10 → 1
- 2⁴=16 > 10, skip → 0
- 2³=8 ≤ 10, use it, remainder = 2 → 1
- 2²=4 > 2, skip → 0
- 2¹=2 ≤ 2, use it, remainder = 0 → 1
- 2⁰=1 > 0, skip → 0

42₁₀ = **0101010₂** = 0x2A

**Method 2: Repeated division by 2**

Divide by 2 and record the remainder. The remainders read bottom-to-top give the binary representation.

42 ÷ 2 = 21 R **0**
21 ÷ 2 = 10 R **1**
10 ÷ 2 = 5  R **0**
5  ÷ 2 = 2  R **1**
2  ÷ 2 = 1  R **0**
1  ÷ 2 = 0  R **1**

Read remainders bottom-to-top: **101010** → with leading zero: **0101010**.

Both methods give the same result. Method 1 is more intuitive for humans; method 2 maps directly to code (it is essentially `n & 1` then `n >>= 1` in a loop).

sections.caption: Greedy subtraction converts decimal 42 to binary 101010 (= 0b101010 = 0x2A).

sections.label: Conversions
sections.explanation: The `n & 1` extracts the last bit (odd/even check), and `n >>= 1` is a right-shift — equivalent to integer division by 2. The loop runs once per bit. Reversing at the end corrects the LSB-first order collected by the loop.

sections.title: Hexadecimal: Compact Binary Shorthand
sections.content:
Binary strings get long fast. A 32-bit memory address looks like `00001010000000000000000000000001` — unreadable. **Hexadecimal (base 16)** is engineers' solution: each hex digit encodes exactly **4 bits** (a nibble), so any binary string can be written four-times more compactly without any information loss.

Hex uses digits 0–9 and letters A–F for values 10–15. So:
- 4 bits `1010` = hex `A` = decimal 10
- 4 bits `1111` = hex `F` = decimal 15
- 8 bits `11001010` = hex `CA` = decimal 202

The conversion is mechanical: split binary into groups of 4 (right-to-left), convert each group independently:

`10111101` → `1011` | `1101` → `B` | `D` → `0xBD`

In code, hex literals are prefixed with `0x` (C, Java, JS, Go) or `0x`/`#` (CSS colours like `#FF5733`). Memory debuggers, network packet dumps, and colour codes are all hex because it makes binary human-readable without losing the one-to-one correspondence with bit patterns.

An important sub-pattern: **0x00 = 0, 0xFF = 255** — these are the byte extremes. `0xFF` appearing in code almost always means "all 8 bits set" or "maximum byte value".

sections.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Binary\n1011 1101"] --> B["Split nibbles\n1011 | 1101"]
  B --> C["Convert each\nB | D"]
  C --> D["Hex: 0xBD"]
sections.caption: Splitting a byte into two nibbles makes hex conversion trivial — no arithmetic needed, just a lookup table.

sections.title: Bytes, Kilobytes, and the Modern Memory Units
sections.content:
**Byte** (8 bits) is the fundamental unit of data storage. Almost all modern memory is byte-addressable — every unique address points to one byte. A char in C is one byte; a pixel in a greyscale image is one byte.

**Powers of 2 create the traditional 'kilo'**: 2¹⁰ = 1024, which is close enough to 1000 that engineers historically called it a kilobyte (KB). This led to decades of confusion:

- **Binary prefixes (IEC standard)**: KiB = 1024 bytes, MiB = 1024 KiB, GiB = 1024 MiB
- **Decimal prefixes (SI standard)**: KB = 1000 bytes, MB = 1000 KB, GB = 1000 MB
- **Hard drives** advertise decimal (larger-sounding number); **operating systems** historically reported binary (smaller number for the same drive)

That is why a '500 GB' drive shows as ~465 GiB in Windows — both are correct in different unit systems.

For programmers, the relevant sizes to memorise:
- 1 byte = 8 bits = values 0–255
- 1 KiB = 1024 bytes (≈ 10³)
- 1 MiB = 1,048,576 bytes (≈ 10⁶)
- 1 GiB = 1,073,741,824 bytes (≈ 10⁹)
- 1 TiB = 1,099,511,627,776 bytes (≈ 10¹²)

A **32-bit** system can address at most 2³² = 4,294,967,296 bytes = **4 GiB** of RAM — the famous 4 GB limit of 32-bit operating systems. A **64-bit** system can address 2⁶⁴ bytes — roughly 18 exabytes — far more than any machine today has.

Common data sizes to build intuition:
- Plain text: ~1 byte per character
- A tweet (280 chars): ~280 bytes → 0.27 KiB
- A paperback book: ~1 MB
- A 4K movie: ~50 GB
- A genome: ~3 GB

sections.title: Bitwise Operations: Operating Directly on Bits
sections.content:
Languages expose the bit level through **bitwise operators**. These work position-by-position on the binary representation of integers:

- `&` (AND): bit is 1 only if both inputs are 1
- `|` (OR): bit is 1 if either input is 1
- `^` (XOR): bit is 1 if inputs differ
- `~` (NOT): flips every bit
- `<<` (left shift): multiply by 2 for each position shifted
- `>>` (right shift): divide by 2 (integer) for each position shifted

Real uses you will encounter in codebases:

**Masking** — isolate specific bits. To extract the lower 4 bits (a nibble): `n & 0x0F`. To extract the upper nibble of a byte: `(n >> 4) & 0x0F`.

**Flag fields** — store multiple boolean flags packed into one integer. Permissions in Unix (`rwxrwxrwx` = 9 bits), CSS `display` flags, WebGL attribute masks. You set a flag with `flags |= BIT`, clear it with `flags &= ~BIT`, and test it with `!!(flags & BIT)`.

**Fast power-of-2 arithmetic** — `n << k` is the same as `n * 2^k` and runs in a single CPU instruction. `n >> k` is integer division by `2^k`. This is why you will see `1 << 10` instead of `1024` in systems code.

**Checking odd/even** — `n & 1` is 1 for odd, 0 for even. Faster than `n % 2` on some architectures (though modern compilers optimise both).

sections.label: Bitwise
sections.code:
// ── Bitwise operations in practice ───────────────────────────

// Flag packing — store 4 boolean flags in one byte
const READ    = 0b0001; // 1
const WRITE   = 0b0010; // 2
const EXECUTE = 0b0100; // 4
const DELETE  = 0b1000; // 8

let perms = 0;
perms |= READ;          // set READ   → 0001
perms |= WRITE;         // set WRITE  → 0011
console.log(perms.toString(2));    // "11"

console.log(!!(perms & READ));     // true  — READ is set
console.log(!!(perms & EXECUTE));  // false — EXECUTE not set

perms &= ~WRITE;        // clear WRITE → 0001
console.log(perms.toString(2));    // "1"

// Nibble extraction from a byte
const byte = 0b10111101; // 0xBD = 189
const lowerNibble = byte & 0x0F;          // 0b1101 = 13 = 0xD
const upperNibble = (byte >> 4) & 0x0F;  // 0b1011 = 11 = 0xB
console.log(upperNibble.toString(16), lowerNibble.toString(16)); // "b" "d"

// Power-of-2 tricks
console.log(1 << 10);  // 1024  (1 KiB)
console.log(1 << 20);  // 1048576  (1 MiB)
console.log(42 & 1);   // 0  — 42 is even
console.log(43 & 1);   // 1  — 43 is odd
sections.explanation: Flag fields are common in systems code and competitive programming. The pattern is: define constants as single-bit values (powers of 2), then use OR to set, AND+NOT to clear, and AND to test. Nibble extraction is exactly what the hex display in a debugger does internally.

sections.title: Common Misconceptions and Edge Cases
sections.content:
**'256 values' vs 'maximum value 255'**: This trips up beginners constantly. An 8-bit unsigned integer has 256 distinct values (0 through 255). The *count* of values is 2⁸ = 256; the *maximum* value is 255 = 2⁸ − 1. Confusing these leads to off-by-one bugs in range checks and array sizes.

**Signed integers and two's complement**: Everything so far assumed unsigned (non-negative) values. Real programs need negative numbers too. The standard encoding is **two's complement**: for an n-bit signed integer, the most significant bit represents −2ⁿ⁻¹ instead of +2ⁿ⁻¹. So an 8-bit signed integer ranges from −128 to +127 — still 256 values, just shifted. Two's complement is clever because addition and subtraction hardware works identically for signed and unsigned; the CPU does not care which interpretation you use.

**Integer overflow**: When you add 1 to the maximum value of an unsigned n-bit integer, it wraps around to 0. In many low-level languages (C, Rust, assembly) this is defined behaviour for unsigned integers. In C, signed overflow is undefined behaviour — a source of real security vulnerabilities.

**Binary vs. text**: Seeing the number 65 in a file could mean the decimal number 65, or the ASCII character 'A' (also encoded as 65). Context — the type of the variable — determines the interpretation. Bits on disk have no inherent meaning; the program reading them decides.

**Historical note:** The word 'bit' was coined by statistician John Tukey in 1947, appearing in a Bell Labs memo. The word 'byte' (8 bits) was coined by Werner Buchholz at IBM around 1956 when designing the IBM Stretch computer. The choice of 8 bits per byte was not inevitable — earlier machines used 6-bit or 7-bit bytes. ASCII itself only needs 7 bits (128 characters). The IBM System/360 in 1964 standardised the 8-bit byte, and the rest of the industry followed.

**Interview and exam traps to know cold:**
- '8 bits store 256 values; the max value is 255' — do not confuse the two.
- 'n bits → 2ⁿ values; adding one bit doubles the range, not adds 1'.
- '1 KB is 1024 bytes in binary context, 1000 in SI' — know the ambiguity exists.
- 'A 32-bit address space limits RAM to 4 GiB' — common OS trivia question.
- '`n & (n-1)` clears the lowest set bit; if the result is 0, n is a power of 2' — classic bit-trick interview question.

items: A **bit** is one binary digit (0 or 1) — the smallest unit of information. 8 bits = 1 byte = 256 distinct values (0–255).
Binary is **base-2 positional notation**: each position is a power of 2 (1, 2, 4, 8, 16 …), doubling left-to-right.
n bits represent **2ⁿ values**; the maximum unsigned value is 2ⁿ − 1; each added bit doubles the range.
Computers use binary because **two-state transistor switches** are cheap, fast, and noise-tolerant — distinguishing only two voltage levels leaves enormous room for error.
**Hexadecimal** (base 16) is compact binary shorthand: one hex digit = 4 bits (a nibble). Conversion is a simple group-and-lookup with no arithmetic.
**Bitwise operators** (`&`, `|`, `^`, `~`, `<<`, `>>`) let you manipulate individual bits — essential for flags, masks, and low-level systems code.
Memory units (KB/MB/GB) have a binary ambiguity (factor 1024) vs decimal (factor 1000); a **32-bit** address space is limited to 4 GiB of RAM.

quiz.question: What is the decimal value of binary 1011?
How many distinct values can 8 bits represent?
quiz.explanation: 2⁸ = 256 distinct values (0 through 255). 255 is the maximum value, not the count of values.

quiz.question: What is the place value of bit position 4 (0-indexed from the right)?
quiz.explanation: Position 4 from the right = 2⁴ = 16. Positions run 2⁰=1, 2¹=2, 2²=4, 2³=8, 2⁴=16.

quiz.question: Why do computers use binary rather than decimal internally?
options: Binary numbers are always shorter than decimal
Two-state switches are physically cheap and noise-tolerant
Binary stores more values per digit than decimal
quiz.explanation: Transistors naturally act as on/off switches. Distinguishing only two voltage states gives enormous noise margins; ten levels would blur together.

quiz.question: Adding one bit to a binary number does what to the count of representable values?
quiz.explanation: 2^(n+1) = 2 × 2ⁿ, so each additional bit doubles the count of distinct values.

quiz.question: How many bits correspond to exactly one hexadecimal digit?
quiz.explanation: Hex digits range 0–15, which requires 4 bits (2⁴=16). This 4-bit group is called a nibble.

quiz.question: What does the bitwise expression `n & 0x0F` do to a byte?
quiz.explanation: 0x0F = 0b00001111. AND-ing with it keeps only the lower 4 bits and zeros the upper 4 — a classic nibble extraction mask.

quiz.question: Why does a 32-bit operating system have a maximum addressable RAM of 4 GiB?
options: 32-bit CPUs can only read 32 bytes at a time
RAM chips are manufactured in 4 GiB units
Operating systems reserve half the address space
quiz.explanation: A 32-bit address bus has 2³² = 4,294,967,296 unique addresses, each pointing to one byte, totalling exactly 4 GiB.
